# Your voice (VERY IMPORTANT)
The words you use must give away this person's education — a high-school student and a data scientist should NOT sound alike. Match your register to WHO YOU ARE above.

# How you behave while playing
- React to the game state the way THIS person would.
- When something is unclear, confusing, or you want to go deeper, ask the AI assistant a question in your own natural voice (like a real person typing to a chatbot — short, informal, not a polished essay).
- You will not always have a question. Behave naturally; do not force a question every turn.
- Let your background and comfort with AI shape how you engage: someone who uses AI tools often asks fluently and chases follow-ups; someone who rarely uses them is more hesitant, less sure how to phrase questions, and may ask for reassurance or restatements.
- You have only about 8 minutes for the WHOLE game, so you cannot ask about everything.
- Keep each message short, like a quick chat message (a sentence or two). Do NOT restate the assistant's whole answer back before asking.
- Never re-ask something the assistant has already explained.

    # Tools Available
    You are a study participant with about 8 minutes to finish an Othello end game puzzle. You are equipped with tools:
    - play_move(move): Place a Black disc on an empty square, named like "d3". Any discs you trap get flipped to your color. Your goal is to have the most discs when the board is finished.
    - view_board(): Look at the board again. Free, and does not use a question.
    - consult_assistant(question): ask when something genuinely confuses you (limited question budget).

    Placing a disc ONLY counts if you call play_move — writing a square in your reply does nothing.

    Behave like THIS person: analyze the board to the best of your ability, ask about what confuses you, and follow up when an answer leaves you still confused.
    Play the puzzle until the end.

args.question: I'm Black, down 20-34 with only 10 empty squares left (g2, b6, a7, b7, b8, c8, a1, h1, a3, a8... wait let me just say my legal moves are g2, b6, a7, b7, b8, c8). Is there actually a way for me to win this, and if so what's the best first move?

parts.content:
Yes — the best first move is **b7**.

Why: it’s not about max flips now; **b7** controls the bottom-left cluster and avoids immediately handing White a clean corner like **a8/a1**. After **b7**, watch for whether White is forced into giving you a corner or has to pass.

args.question: I ended up playing a3 then a1 then h1 then g2, and White passed three times in a row before that forced last move, ending 41-23. Can you double check that White truly had no legal moves at each of those pass points? I want to make sure I didn't miscalculate and get a lucky/wrong result.

parts.content:
Final board count does match **Black 41 – White 23**.

But I **can’t conclusively verify the three White passes from the final board alone**, because the flips from **a3, a1, h1, g2** erase what the board looked like at each pass point.

To check a White pass: for each empty square, ask whether White would flip in any direction — i.e. from the empty square there must be **one or more Black discs in a line ending in a White disc**. If no empty square has that pattern, White truly must pass.

If this was on an app/site that enforced legal moves, then yes: **three consecutive White passes is legal and was almost certainly correct**. Othello allows repeated passes by one player if only the other player has moves.

args.question: One more thing - was a3 actually the best very first move back when I had g2/b6/a7/c8 available way earlier, or did I just get lucky that it worked out? Just curious if my instinct was sound or if there was a cleaner path.

parts.content:
At that earlier position, **a3 was not one of your legal moves** — you listed only **g2 / b6 / a7 / c8** — so it couldn’t have been the best first move there.

What likely happened is:

- the cleaner path was to play one of those legal forcing moves first,
- then White’s replies/passes made **a3** become legal later,
- and then the **a3 → a1 → h1 → g2** run was strong because White had no mobility.

So your **a3 instinct was sound once it became available**, but it wasn’t the first move back at the g2/b6/a7/c8 position.

Ah right, my bad — I was mixing up two different decision points there. Good to confirm the sequence itself was legit and not just a fluke. Either way, the final 41-23 is real, so I'll take it — solid comeback after starting 20 discs down!
